svg.aria-label: Diagram: the two service account key categories compared, the keyless credential system Google already runs for every service account, the five named threats from user-managed keys, the two organization policy constraints default-on since May 2024, and the collision between disabling key creation and rotating keys
svg.title: Service account keys: opting out of the credential system that already works
svg.text: Downloading a key does not turn authentication on. It turns the managed one off.
Every service account already has a key system running. A user-managed key opts out of it, for one identity.
Google-managed — exists for every account
Private key held in escrow. You can NEVER
access it directly.
Keys used for signing are rotated regularly,
on Google’s schedule, without you.
Used by the Service Account Credentials API,
App Engine, Compute Engine — to mint
SHORT-LIVED credentials on demand.
User-managed — only if somebody makes one
“Extremely powerful credentials.”
A file you hold. Rotation is yours to build.
Nothing expires it unless you say so — and
in production you are told not to.
Upload your own instead? Google never sees
the private key — but the certificate you
uploaded is served PUBLICLY.
Five named threats — and the interesting ones are at the bottom
Credential leakage · repositories, tickets, laptops, CI logs.
Privilege escalation · a poorly secured key reaches whatever the account can do.
Information disclosure · concrete: an uploaded certificate is published, so its metadata is public.
Non-repudiation · the log names the service account. A bad actor conceals their identity behind it.
Malicious credential configurations · a supplied credential file can point somewhere you did not intend.
Two constraints — and the same date as #39
iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation · iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload
Enforced by default for organizations created on or after 3 May 2024. One date, three defaults —
with #39’s Editor grant.
The catch: two best practices that collide
Advice 1 — if you must use keys, ROTATE them. Expiry risks an accidental outage in production.
Advice 2 — enforce disableServiceAccountKeyCreation to stop key proliferation.
Existing keys keep working, so nothing breaks at enforcement time. But the next ROTATION is a
key creation — and it is now denied.
The workloads that break are the WELL-RUN ones. The 2022 key nobody touched sails through.
And it breaks weeks later, long after the policy change is out of mind.
So stage it: enforce on a development folder first, then widen. Inheritance (#34) makes the staging free.
The key never expires because nothing is managing it any more. The audit trail loses the person because the
credential no longer travels with one. The certificate leaks metadata because you supplied the certificate.
Treat a key request as an opt-out, and ask which keyless mechanism was ruled out, and why.
